name: Zoe Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me what you actually did at work yesterday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A sports hall gave me four different ticket totals for the same Saturday, so I spent the morning finding which refunds had crossed into Monday's bank deposit. I'm 43, an experienced mid-level accountant at Hill & Fern, about average at the job, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I like explaining a messy number to the volunteer who runs the hall; I dislike an answer that looks neat but has the wrong date under it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do the evenings and the family budget look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ben teaches at a primary school, and our children are seven and eleven; one of us is usually packing a lunch while the other checks homework. My pay is typical for accounting, we have five months of expenses saved, a mortgage and some other firms nearby. I use AI every day to group ticket payments and draft questions, then check the bank trail myself. I try new tools quickly, but I don't join a camp on every policy question; I want to know whose time and money a change uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster ticket sort is useful if we keep the refund trail open for the hall. I'd show the volunteer the Monday bank entry before claiming the account balances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages and five months saved make the mortgage feel steady. I think my role stays, and the small AI gains might give me an evening back with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for a first ticket grouping and compare each refund with the bank statement. In the first year I'd put seventy a month from pay into our emergency account and keep the family swimming lesson as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the bills. A quieter Friday would be welcome, but I would still check the refunds myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error did you catch last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cancelled match was counted as both a refund and a new sale. The bank entry showed only the refund, so I fixed the hall's return before filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not before the partners show what it catches on old ticket files. I use the approved one daily. More buttons are not always more evidence.

say: I would show volunteers the **bank trail** behind ticket refunds.
I would keep a **human review** of every odd entry.
think: My **role seems stable** with two wages and five months saved.
A small time gain could return a **family evening**.
do: Keep checking **ticket refunds** against the bank statement after daily AI grouping.
Save **seventy monthly** from pay into the emergency account.
feel: She feels **calm** about bills while still checking the source.
S0.quote: More buttons are not always more evidence.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily**, then follows the bank trail for exceptions.
With five months saved and a teacher’s wage at home, she can keep **swimming lessons** during a plateau.

steps.text: Keep checking ticket refunds against bank entries after daily AI grouping
Add seventy monthly from pay to household emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hill & Fern to show us the errors as well as the quicker file times. A system that drafts the client email should not quietly decide what a volunteer is told.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my work is checking and explaining figures, so I expect the firm to reduce at least one review shift in our small team. It might be my shift, although five months saved and Ben's school wage give us time to respond.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for a paid old-file trial with a senior reviewer, comparing twenty sports-hall returns and logging bad refund suggestions. In the first year of steady change, if my hours fall, I'd apply for posted finance jobs at the local venues and keep any funded Hill & Fern hours until I have a written salary and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because my own wage could shrink. I can move quickly with a tool, but I cannot make a new employer pay quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm won't pay for the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using our approved daily sorter and my bank check, and ask the partners for the staffing schedule. I would not do new client testing on unpaid nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which venue role would you actually seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An advertised accounts officer post with a stated wage and school-hours fit, not a vague promise to call me. Ben can do pickup if his class ends on time, but we'd check that before I accept.

say: I would compare **errors and speed** before changing the review rota.
I would keep a **named human** behind client emails.
think: At least **one review shift** may go, possibly mine.
Five months saved gives us **search time**, not replacement wages.
do: Run a **paid twenty-file trial** with senior review if approved.
Keep **approved sorting checks** if new trial funding is refused.
Apply for **posted venue finance** work if my hours fall.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a cut to her own wage.
S1.quote: I can move quickly with a tool, but I cannot make a new employer pay quickly.
fieldNote: She uses fast tool learning but requires **paid old-file testing** and a refund error log.
A new venue role needs **written pay** and a start date fitting school hours; she keeps firm pay meanwhile.

steps.text: Test twenty old sports-hall returns on paid time with senior review if approved
Keep approved ticket sorting and bank checks if new trial refused
Apply for posted venue finance jobs after hour cut; require written salary start and pickup fit
Keep funded Hill and Fern hours until written salary and start date are confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that full AGI in 2028 reaches the accounts desk before robots touch hands-on work around 2031. Hill & Fern should show us which fees still pay for a reviewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our sports-hall accounts fee to fall sharply when AGI can do the figures cheaply, and my paid role could go. Ben's teaching wage might hold, but it does not cover the mortgage and two children alone for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the planned new garden room and put its monthly two-hundred payment into cash savings now. In the first year after 2028, if Hill & Fern ends my role, I'd apply for advertised salaried finance jobs at nearby schools and take only a confirmed paid weekend class for traders if Ben can cover the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing my own wage. Five months saved is useful, but it is not a plan for the rest of my working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the class teach, and who would pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd teach a trader to separate cash received from profit using their own figures, in a rented library room. I'd run it only if six people pay a fee that covers the room and my travel; it would be my own weekend income, with Hill & Fern's client files left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only two traders pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the room booking and keep looking for a salaried school role. Ben would not give up a Saturday with the children for a class that loses money.

say: I would ask which **fees fund review** after AGI reaches the desk.
I would distinguish **2028 desk risk** from later robots.
think: My **sports-hall fee** may collapse when AGI makes the figures cheap, taking my wage.
Ben’s **teacher pay** cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: Save **two hundred monthly** by delaying the garden room.
Apply for **advertised school finance** jobs if my role ends.
Run a **paid trader class** only with six buyers and childcare covered.
feel: She feels **alarmed** about losing a whole wage.
S2.quote: Five months saved is useful, but it is not a plan for the rest of my working life.
fieldNote: She tests her own **weekend income** only at a fee that covers room and travel, without using employer clients.
A two-person class triggers **cancellation**, while the salaried school search continues.

steps.text: Delay garden room and add two hundred monthly to cash savings
Apply for advertised salaried school finance job after 2028 role loss
Run own library trader class only if six pay room and travel and Ben covers children
Cancel library room if fewer than six traders pay; continue salaried search

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to find whether small traders will pay to understand their own accounts, and whether venues still want a person checking refunds. A good idea needs receipts from paying people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I'd still need a mortgage wage, and AGI may handle the ticket accounts that fill my week. The class might be a small second income, not a substitute for my salary, so I would keep looking at posted finance roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try one Saturday trader class next spring only if six pay in advance, the library room and travel are covered, and Ben is home with the children. In the first year after 2031, if Hill & Fern cuts my salaried hours, I'd keep any paid firm work and apply for posted school finance roles with a written wage and start date; I'd run a second class only if the first covers its costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years allows a small test without gambling our mortgage reserve. I won't call a class a new career after one Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to repeat the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count the six paid places and then ask whether four would pay for another lesson. If only two return, I would stop booking the room and put my Saturday back with the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no school finance vacancy appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep funded Hill & Fern hours and the five-month reserve for bills. I would not leave a salary for a mailing list of possible openings.

say: I would test **six paid places** before booking a room.
I would require **four repeat buyers** before a second lesson.
think: At **48 in 2031**, I still need a mortgage wage.
A **weekend class** may help but cannot replace salary.
do: Run **one paid trader class** with six prepaid places and Ben covering children.
Repeat only if **four traders** pay again and costs are covered.
Apply for **posted school finance** work if firm salary falls after 2031.
feel: She feels **anxious**, but can test paid demand without risking savings.
S3.quote: I won't call a class a new career after one Saturday.
fieldNote: She calls the class **personal weekend income** and protects the firm’s files and household reserve.
Her second class needs **four repeat buyers**; a job move needs written pay and a real opening.

steps.text: Run paid Saturday trader class only with six prepaid places costs covered and Ben home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives the children time to finish school and gives us time to clear some mortgage debt. I would still ask whether clients buy an explanation after a machine makes the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I would need wages even if our children are older. AGI reaches the accounts desk then, and the ten-year delay helps only if I put real cash against the loan before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay one hundred and twenty extra monthly off mortgage principal while both wages hold and teach an initial short weekend trader class only when six pay enough to cover room and travel. In the first year after 2036, if Hill & Fern cuts my salaried role, I'd apply for a posted school finance job with written pay and a start date, keeping any funded firm hours until it begins. I would book a second lesson only if paying repeat buyers cover the room and travel again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, because ten years could leave a smaller loan but I would still need work at 53. My weekend accounts class is useful only if traders pay for another lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ben's teaching wage falls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra principal payment and keep cash for food and bills. I wouldn't use the children's school fund to keep a class open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot date around 2039 change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the accounts desk is thinking work and changes in 2036. Robots around 2039 may affect other jobs later, but they don't postpone my pay risk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the accounts fee could vanish before the mortgage is smaller. A posted school finance job with written wages and an honest fee breakdown from the firm would help. I can teach a trader how to read a bank statement, but I cannot teach a missing salary to arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is checking a volunteer's return when software says the ticket sales match. A refund can cross a weekend and look like a missing sale if nobody opens the bank page.

headlineQuote: I can teach a trader how to read a bank statement, but I cannot teach a missing salary to arrive.
portrait: Zoe, **43**, is an experienced average-skilled accountant at Hill & Fern with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
Her **typical pay**, five-month reserve and Ben’s teaching wage support two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses AI **daily** on sports-hall ticket records, with some nearby firms if a salary search becomes necessary.
She fears **2028 role loss** and tests her own paid weekend class while preserving school finance as a wage path.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her fee-funded role before the family reduces its mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted school finance job** with written wages and an honest firm fee breakdown would help.
